title: Module Overview: Five Platonic Solids, One Zero Dehn Invariant
content:
The module header presents the complete classification table in ASCII form — a rare and pedagogically valuable practice that makes the main result immediately visible before the proof begins. The table shows all five Platonic solids with their edge counts and dihedral angles, marking only the cube with 'D = 0'.

The docstring also presents the key mathematical argument in outline: for arccos(-1/√5) (dodecahedron angle), the irrationality propagates through a chain 3/5 → 1/√5 → -1/√5 via the half-angle identity 2·arccos(1/√5) = π - arccos(3/5). The Chebyshev sequence d_n = 5^n · 2cos(n·arccos(3/5)) is introduced at the docstring level, setting up the proof before the formal code begins.

The axiom budget section explicitly accounts for both assumptions: tmul_infinite_order_ne_zero (inherited from OQ02OQ02, needed for the tensor product Dehn invariant to detect nonzero elements) and icoAngle_irrational (icosahedron, deferred). This transparency about axiom accounting is a hallmark of honest formalization practice.
mathContext: The five Platonic solids (V, E, F with V-E+F=2): Cube (8,12,6; π/2), Tetrahedron (4,6,4; arccos(1/3)), Octahedron (6,12,8; arccos(-1/3)), Dodecahedron (20,30,12; arccos(-1/√5)), Icosahedron (12,30,20; arccos(-√5/3)). Dehn invariant D(P) = Σ_e len(e) ⊗ [θ(e)] ∈ ℝ ⊗_ℤ (ℝ/πℤ). A dihedral angle θ satisfies [θ] = 0 in ℝ/πℤ iff θ/π ∈ ℚ. The cube's angle π/2 has π/2 ÷ π = 1/2 ∈ ℚ, giving D = 0. All other angles are irrational multiples of π.

title: Chebyshev Sequence Design: Clearing √5 Denominators
content: The sequence cosThreeFifthsSeq is engineered so that d_n = 5^n · 2cos(n·arccos(3/5)) is always an integer, despite cos(arccos(3/5)) = 3/5 being rational with denominator 5. Multiplying by 5^n clears all denominators from the Chebyshev evaluation: the recurrence d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n has integer coefficients 6 = 2·(6/5)·5 and 25 = 5². This parallels nivenSeq in OQ02, where multiplying by 3^n cleared the 1/3 denominator from arccos(1/3).
mathContext: For cos θ = 3/5, the Chebyshev recurrence 2cos((n+2)θ) = 2cosθ · 2cos((n+1)θ) − 2cos(nθ) gives: 5^{n+2} · 2cos((n+2)θ) = 6 · [5^{n+1} · 2cos((n+1)θ)] − 25 · [5^n · 2cos(nθ)]. The key: 5^{n+2} · 2cosθ = 5^{n+2} · 6/5 = 6 · 5^{n+1}, so all factors of 5 cancel into integer coefficients.

title: Mod-5 Divisibility: Parallel to OQ02's Mod-3 Argument
content: The proof that 5 ∤ cosThreeFifthsSeq n exactly mirrors the proof that 3 ∤ nivenSeq n in OQ02. The recurrence d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} − 25d_n reduces mod 5 to d_{n+2} ≡ d_{n+1} (mod 5) — since 6 ≡ 1 and 25 ≡ 0. So the non-divisibility propagates: from 5 ∤ d_n and 5 ∤ d_{n+1}, we derive 5 ∤ d_{n+2}. The base: d_0 = 2, d_1 = 6 — neither divisible by 5.
mathContext: If 5 | d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} − 25d_n, then since 5 | 25d_n we get 5 | 6d_{n+1}. Since gcd(5,6) = 1 (5 is prime, 5 ∤ 6), we get 5 | d_{n+1} — contradicting the inductive hypothesis. The proof uses `Prime (5 : ℤ)` and `Prime.dvd_or_dvd` to factor the divisibility.

title: Half-Angle Identity: 2·arccos(1/√5) = arccos(-3/5)
content: The proof computes cos(2·arccos(1/√5)) = 2·(1/√5)² − 1 = 2/5 − 1 = −3/5, then uses Real.arccos_cos to identify the angle: since 2·arccos(1/√5) ∈ [0, π] (because arccos(1/√5) ≤ π/2, which holds since 1/√5 ≥ 0), and its cosine equals −3/5, it must equal arccos(−3/5). The key Mathlib fact: arccos_le_pi_div_two says arccos x ≤ π/2 iff x ≥ 0.
mathContext: Proof: arccos_cos(h₁: 0 ≤ 2θ)(h₂: 2θ ≤ π): arccos(cos(2θ)) = 2θ. With 2θ = 2·arccos(1/√5): need 0 ≤ 2·arccos(1/√5) (trivial by nonnegativity of arccos) and 2·arccos(1/√5) ≤ π (from arccos(1/√5) ≤ π/2 since 1/√5 ≥ 0). Then cos(2·arccos(1/√5)) = 2(1/√5)² − 1 = −3/5 (using √5·√5 = 5).

title: Chain of Irrational Angles: 3/5 → 1/√5 → -1/√5
content: The irrationality propagates through a three-step chain. First, arccos(3/5)/π ∉ ℚ (proved via cosThreeFifthsSeq). Second, if arccos(1/√5)/π = r ∈ ℚ, then arccos(3/5)/π = 1 − 2r ∈ ℚ (using 2·arccos(1/√5) = π − arccos(3/5)), contradiction. Third, if arccos(-1/√5)/π = r ∈ ℚ, then arccos(1/√5)/π = 1 − r ∈ ℚ (using arccos(-x) = π − arccos(x)), contradiction. Each step is a simple rational arithmetic consequence.
mathContext: Chain: arccos(3/5)/π ∉ ℚ → arccos(1/√5)/π ∉ ℚ → arccos(-1/√5)/π ∉ ℚ. The implications use: (1) 2·arccos(1/√5) + arccos(3/5) = π [half-angle identity + arccos_neg], (2) arccos(-1/√5) + arccos(1/√5) = π [arccos_neg]. If any of the latter were rational p/q ∈ ℚ, rationality propagates back to arccos(3/5)/π ∉ ℚ.

title: Strong Induction: Proving the Cosine Relation d_n = 5^n · 2cos(n·arccos(3/5))
content:
The proof of cosThreeFifthsSeq_eq_cos uses Lean's paired strong induction: to prove P(n) for all n, it suffices to prove P(n) ∧ P(n+1) by induction. This naturally handles recurrences where each step depends on the two preceding values.

Base cases (n=0): d_0 = 2 = 5^0 · 2cos(0) (trivial by cos_zero) and d_1 = 6 = 5^1 · 2cos(arccos(3/5)) = 5 · 2 · (3/5) = 6 (using cos(arccos(3/5)) = 3/5 from arccos_cos).

Inductive step: Given d_n = 5^n · 2cos(n·θ) and d_{n+1} = 5^{n+1} · 2cos((n+1)·θ), prove d_{n+2} = 5^{n+2} · 2cos((n+2)·θ). The proof uses `cos_step` (Chebyshev addition: 2cos((n+2)θ) = (6/5)·2cos((n+1)θ) - 2cos(nθ)) combined with the recurrence d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n.
mathContext: The cosine addition formula: $2\cos((n+2)\theta) = 2\cos\theta \cdot 2\cos((n+1)\theta) - 2\cos(n\theta)$. With $\theta = \arccos(3/5)$ so $2\cos\theta = 6/5$: $2\cos((n+2)\theta) = (6/5) \cdot 2\cos((n+1)\theta) - 2\cos(n\theta)$. Multiplying by $5^{n+2}$: $5^{n+2} \cdot 2\cos((n+2)\theta) = 6 \cdot [5^{n+1} \cdot 2\cos((n+1)\theta)] - 25 \cdot [5^n \cdot 2\cos(n\theta)] = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n = d_{n+2}$.

title: From Angle Irrationality to Nonzero Dehn Invariant
content:
Parts III and IV apply the Dehn-Sydler infrastructure from OQ02OQ02 to conclude that the dodecahedron and icosahedron have nonzero Dehn invariants. The logical structure is uniform for all non-cube Platonic solids:

1. **Angle irrationality** → **Infinite order in ℝ/πℤ**: `dodAngle_infinite_order` shows that for all nonzero integers n, n·[arccos(-1/√5)] ≠ 0 in ℝ/πℤ. This is derived directly from dodAngle_irrational: if n·[θ] = 0, then [θ] = 0, meaning θ/π ∈ ℚ, contradicting irrationality.

2. **Infinite order + flatness** → **Nonzero tensor product**: `dod_dehn_ne_zero` applies `tmul_infinite_order_ne_zero` (the flatness axiom from OQ02OQ02): if the angle class has infinite order and the edge length is positive, then `edgeTerm (30a) dodAngle ≠ 0`.

The icosahedron case (Part IV) is identical in structure, using the axiomatized `icoAngle_irrational` instead of the proved dodecahedron irrationality. This uniform two-step argument (irrationality → infinite order → nonzero tensor) is the Dehn invariant method in its most transparent form.
mathContext: $D(\text{dodecahedron}) = 30a \otimes [\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})]$ in $\mathbb{R} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} (\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z})$. The edge term $\text{edgeTerm}(30a, \theta) = 30a \otimes [\theta]$. Since $[\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})]$ has infinite order in $\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$ and $30a > 0$, the flatness axiom gives $30a \otimes [\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})] \neq 0$. The flatness of $\mathbb{R}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is the key: for a flat module $M$, $m \otimes x = 0$ iff $x$ is torsion — i.e., $nx = 0$ for some nonzero $n$. Since $[\theta]$ has infinite order (no torsion), the tensor is nonzero.

title: Axiom Audit and Sorries: Honest Accounting
content:
The final section provides an explicit axiom audit — a practice that exemplifies good formalization hygiene. The 2 axioms are clearly categorized:

**New axiom** (introduced here): `icoAngle_irrational` — arccos(-√5/3)/π ∉ ℚ. The docstring explains the planned proof approach (Chebyshev arithmetic in ℤ[√5] with a mod-3 argument) and why it was deferred (ℤ[√5] arithmetic complexity). This is a principled deferral, not an unexplained sorry.

**Inherited axiom** (from OQ02OQ02): `tmul_infinite_order_ne_zero` — ℝ flat over ℤ. This is a standard algebraic fact about ℝ as a torsion-free (hence flat) ℤ-module, expected to be formalizable from Mathlib's `Module.Flat` API.

The 3 sorries in `cube_unique_zero_dehn` are structural (general edge-count scaling lemmas that don't affect the main classification theorem `cube_isolated_dehn_invariant`). The `#check` commands at the end verify that the key theorems type-check, providing a final sanity check.

The ratio of proved-to-axiomatized is 11 theorems proved vs. 2 axioms — a healthy ratio for a file extending the boundaries of what Mathlib directly supports.
mathContext: The flatness of $\mathbb{R}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ follows from $\mathbb{R}$ being torsion-free ($n \cdot x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0$ for nonzero integers $n$) and the equivalence: a $\mathbb{Z}$-module is flat iff it is torsion-free (since $\mathbb{Z}$ is a PID). This is the foundational content of `tmul_infinite_order_ne_zero`: for torsion-free $\mathbb{R}$, $r \otimes x = 0$ (in $\mathbb{R} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} M$) only if $r = 0$ or $x$ is a torsion element of $M$.

title: Complete Platonic Solid Classification
content: The theorem cube_isolated_dehn_invariant packages the complete 5-solid classification into a single conjunction. The cube (12 edges, π/2 dihedral) has D = 0; all other Platonic solids have D ≠ 0. The tetrahedron and octahedron results come from OQ02OQ02; the dodecahedron is new in this file; the icosahedron uses the axiomatized angle irrationality. The classification has an immediate geometric consequence: no scissors-congruence exists between the cube and any other Platonic solid.
mathContext: Five Platonic solids (V-E+F = 2): Cube (8-12+6=2, π/2), Tetrahedron (4-6+4=2, arccos(1/3)), Octahedron (6-12+8=2, arccos(-1/3)), Dodecahedron (20-30+12=2, arccos(-1/√5)), Icosahedron (12-30+20=2, arccos(-√5/3)). All non-cube angles are irrational multiples of π, giving nonzero Dehn invariants. The cube's angle π/2 = (1/2)π is rational, giving D = 0.
